title: Clinical Microbiology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 400L Clinical Microbiology curriculum: specimen collection and processing, normal flora versus pathogens, clinical syndromes and their common causative agents (UTI, bacteraemia/sepsis, meningitis, pneumonia, wound infection, gastroenteritis), diagnostic workflow (culture, biochemical/serological identification, susceptibility testing), and clinical laboratory quality practice -- distinct from MCB306's population-level public health focus.

questions.question: In clinical microbiology, 'normal flora' refers to microorganisms that:
options: Always cause disease when present on or in the human body

Routinely colonise specific body sites of healthy individuals without causing disease, and may even play protective roles, but can cause infection if they reach a normally sterile site or the host becomes compromised
Are found exclusively in hospital environments
Can only be bacteria, never fungi
questions.correct_answer: Routinely colonise specific body sites of healthy individuals without causing disease, and may even play protective roles, but can cause infection if they reach a normally sterile site or the host becomes compromised
questions.explanation: Normal (resident) flora colonises sites such as skin, gut, and mucous membranes without causing harm in a healthy host, and can even help exclude pathogens, but members of the normal flora can become opportunistic pathogens if translocated to a sterile site or if host defences are weakened.

questions.question: Which body sites/fluids are normally considered sterile in a healthy individual, such that isolation of any bacteria from them is clinically significant?
options: Skin and the mouth
Cerebrospinal fluid and blood
The large intestine
The upper respiratory tract
questions.correct_answer: Cerebrospinal fluid and blood
questions.explanation: Cerebrospinal fluid, blood, and other deep tissue/body fluids are normally sterile; recovery of bacteria from these sites is generally interpreted as clinically significant infection rather than contamination or normal colonisation, unlike skin or gut sites which harbour abundant normal flora.

questions.question: For a midstream urine specimen submitted for culture in suspected urinary tract infection, a bacterial colony count of ≥10^5 CFU/mL of a single predominant organism is classically interpreted as:
options: Definite contamination and should be discarded
Significant bacteriuria, consistent with true urinary tract infection rather than contamination
Always a false-positive result
Evidence of a viral infection
questions.correct_answer: Significant bacteriuria, consistent with true urinary tract infection rather than contamination
questions.explanation: The classic Kass criterion of ≥10^5 CFU/mL of a single organism in a properly collected midstream urine specimen is used as the threshold to distinguish clinically significant bacteriuria (true infection) from likely contamination by periurethral flora, though lower counts may still be significant in symptomatic patients or with certain collection methods.

questions.question: The most common causative organism of uncomplicated community-acquired urinary tract infection is:
options: Escherichia coli (uropathogenic strains)
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Treponema pallidum
Clostridioides difficile
questions.correct_answer: Escherichia coli (uropathogenic strains)
questions.explanation: Uropathogenic Escherichia coli, which ascends from the periurethral/gut flora and possesses virulence factors such as adhesins (P-fimbriae) for uroepithelial attachment, is responsible for the large majority of uncomplicated community-acquired urinary tract infections.

questions.question: Blood cultures for suspected bacteraemia/septicaemia should ideally be collected:
options: As a single sample, regardless of timing

As two or more separate sets from different venepuncture sites, ideally before antimicrobial therapy is started, to improve sensitivity and help distinguish true bacteraemia from skin-flora contamination
Only after the patient has completed a full course of antibiotics
Using a used needle to save cost
questions.correct_answer: As two or more separate sets from different venepuncture sites, ideally before antimicrobial therapy is started, to improve sensitivity and help distinguish true bacteraemia from skin-flora contamination
questions.explanation: Collecting multiple blood culture sets from different sites (before antibiotics are given, whenever feasible) increases the chance of detecting intermittent or low-grade bacteraemia and helps differentiate a true pathogen (recovered in multiple sets) from a skin-flora contaminant (typically recovered in only one set).

questions.question: Isolation of coagulase-negative Staphylococcus (e.g. S. epidermidis) from only one of several blood culture bottles drawn from a patient without indwelling devices most often represents:
options: Definite true bacteraemia requiring immediate aggressive treatment
Likely skin-flora contamination introduced during venepuncture, rather than true infection
Evidence of tuberculosis
A laboratory error that cannot be interpreted
questions.correct_answer: Likely skin-flora contamination introduced during venepuncture, rather than true infection
questions.explanation: Coagulase-negative staphylococci are common skin flora and frequent blood culture contaminants; when recovered from only a single bottle out of multiple sets in a patient without risk factors like indwelling catheters, contamination is far more likely than true bacteraemia, though clinical correlation is always required.

questions.question: In a case of suspected bacterial meningitis, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis typically shows, compared with normal CSF:
options: Decreased white cell count, increased glucose, decreased protein
Increased (often markedly elevated, neutrophil-predominant) white cell count, decreased glucose, and increased protein
No change in any parameter
Increased glucose only, with normal cell count and protein
questions.correct_answer: Increased (often markedly elevated, neutrophil-predominant) white cell count, decreased glucose, and increased protein
questions.explanation: Bacterial meningitis classically produces a CSF neutrophilic pleocytosis, low CSF glucose (as bacteria and neutrophils consume it) relative to blood glucose, and elevated protein (from increased blood-brain barrier permeability), a pattern that helps distinguish it from viral meningitis.

questions.question: Neisseria meningitidis, a major cause of bacterial meningitis particularly in the African 'meningitis belt' including parts of Nigeria, is characteristically seen on Gram stain of CSF as:
options: Gram-negative diplococci, often intracellular within neutrophils
Gram-positive cocci in chains
Gram-positive rods forming spores
Acid-fast bacilli
questions.correct_answer: Gram-negative diplococci, often intracellular within neutrophils
questions.explanation: Neisseria meningitidis appears on Gram stain as Gram-negative diplococci (kidney/coffee-bean shaped pairs), frequently seen phagocytosed within polymorphonuclear leukocytes in CSF from patients with meningococcal meningitis.

questions.question: Streptococcus pneumoniae, a leading cause of community-acquired bacterial pneumonia and meningitis, characteristically appears on Gram stain as:
options: Gram-positive diplococci, often lancet-shaped
Gram-negative rods
Gram-positive branching filaments
Gram-negative curved rods
questions.correct_answer: Gram-positive diplococci, often lancet-shaped
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae typically appears as Gram-positive, lancet (flame)-shaped diplococci, a key morphological clue on direct Gram stain of sputum or CSF that supports a presumptive diagnosis pending culture confirmation.

questions.question: The optochin susceptibility test is used in the clinical laboratory to help differentiate:
options: Streptococcus pneumoniae (optochin-susceptible) from other alpha-haemolytic streptococci such as viridans streptococci (optochin-resistant)
Gram-positive from Gram-negative bacteria
Staphylococcus aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci
Aerobes from anaerobes
questions.correct_answer: Streptococcus pneumoniae (optochin-susceptible) from other alpha-haemolytic streptococci such as viridans streptococci (optochin-resistant)
questions.explanation: Optochin (ethylhydrocupreine hydrochloride) selectively inhibits Streptococcus pneumoniae, producing a zone of inhibition around an optochin disc, whereas other alpha-haemolytic (viridans) streptococci are resistant, making this a rapid, inexpensive differentiating test.

questions.question: In a sputum sample submitted for bacterial culture, the presence of many squamous epithelial cells and few polymorphonuclear leukocytes on Gram stain generally suggests:
options: An excellent, representative lower respiratory tract specimen
Significant contamination with oral/upper respiratory secretions, making the specimen unsuitable for reliable interpretation
Active tuberculosis
A definitively negative culture will follow
questions.correct_answer: Significant contamination with oral/upper respiratory secretions, making the specimen unsuitable for reliable interpretation
questions.explanation: Squamous epithelial cells originate from the oropharynx, so their abundance (with few neutrophils) on a pre-culture Gram stain screen indicates the sample is contaminated with saliva rather than representative of lower respiratory tract secretions, and such specimens are often rejected or reported with caution.

questions.question: Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) staining is used in the clinical laboratory primarily to detect:
options: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and other mycobacteria, whose waxy, mycolic-acid-rich cell walls resist decolourisation by acid-alcohol after carbol fuchsin staining
Gram-positive cocci
Fungal spores
Viral inclusion bodies
questions.correct_answer: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and other mycobacteria, whose waxy, mycolic-acid-rich cell walls resist decolourisation by acid-alcohol after carbol fuchsin staining
questions.explanation: Mycobacteria have a lipid-rich, mycolic-acid cell wall that retains the primary carbol fuchsin stain even after treatment with acid-alcohol decolouriser, appearing as bright red/pink 'acid-fast' bacilli against a blue methylene-blue counterstained background, a key diagnostic feature for tuberculosis screening.

questions.question: In stool culture for bacterial enteric pathogens, selective/differential media such as MacConkey, Salmonella-Shigella (SS), or Xylose Lysine Deoxycholate (XLD) agar are used mainly to:
options: Grow all intestinal organisms equally well without any selection
Suppress or slow the growth of normal faecal flora while allowing differentiation and easier recognition of potential enteric pathogens such as Salmonella and Shigella
Sterilise the stool sample
Identify viral gastroenteritis
questions.correct_answer: Suppress or slow the growth of normal faecal flora while allowing differentiation and easier recognition of potential enteric pathogens such as Salmonella and Shigella
questions.explanation: Selective/differential stool culture media contain inhibitory agents (e.g. bile salts) that suppress much of the normal faecal flora while permitting growth of enteric pathogens, combined with indicators that help distinguish lactose-fermenting from non-fermenting colonies, streamlining recovery of pathogens like Salmonella and Shigella.

questions.question: A surgical wound swab that grows a heavy, pure culture of Staphylococcus aureus from a wound with clinical signs of inflammation (redness, pus, warmth) is best interpreted as:
options: Definite contamination with no clinical relevance
Likely true wound infection, given the clinical correlation with local signs of inflammation and a pure, heavy growth of a recognised pathogen
Evidence the patient has tuberculosis
Proof of a fungal infection
questions.correct_answer: Likely true wound infection, given the clinical correlation with local signs of inflammation and a pure, heavy growth of a recognised pathogen
questions.explanation: Clinical microbiology interpretation always requires correlating laboratory findings with the clinical picture; a heavy, pure growth of a recognised pathogen from a wound showing clinical signs of infection supports a diagnosis of true infection rather than incidental colonisation or contamination.

questions.question: An antibiogram (antibiotic susceptibility report) is generated in the clinical laboratory by:
options: Testing the identified pathogen against a panel of relevant antimicrobial agents and reporting it as susceptible, intermediate, or resistant to guide appropriate treatment
Simply culturing the organism without further testing
Reporting only the Gram stain result
Measuring the patient's white blood cell count
questions.correct_answer: Testing the identified pathogen against a panel of relevant antimicrobial agents and reporting it as susceptible, intermediate, or resistant to guide appropriate treatment
questions.explanation: After a pathogen is isolated and identified, susceptibility testing (e.g. disc diffusion or automated MIC methods) against a relevant panel of antibiotics produces an antibiogram, which clinicians use to select appropriate, effective antimicrobial therapy.

questions.question: Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacteriaceae are of major clinical concern because these enzymes:
options: Are inactive against all beta-lactam antibiotics
Hydrolyse a broad range of beta-lactam antibiotics, including penicillins and most cephalosporins, conferring resistance and often necessitating carbapenem therapy
Only affect Gram-positive organisms
Increase susceptibility to all antibiotics
questions.correct_answer: Hydrolyse a broad range of beta-lactam antibiotics, including penicillins and most cephalosporins, conferring resistance and often necessitating carbapenem therapy
questions.explanation: ESBLs are enzymes, often plasmid-encoded, that hydrolyse and inactivate a wide range of beta-lactam antibiotics including penicillins, cephalosporins, and monobactams, conferring multidrug resistance that frequently limits treatment options to carbapenems or other alternative agents.

questions.question: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), an important cause of both hospital- and community-acquired infections, is defined by resistance mediated primarily by:
options: Production of beta-lactamase alone
Acquisition of the mecA (or mecC) gene, encoding an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) with reduced affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics
Loss of the bacterial cell wall entirely
A mutation preventing any protein synthesis
questions.correct_answer: Acquisition of the mecA (or mecC) gene, encoding an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) with reduced affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics
questions.explanation: MRSA resistance is driven mainly by the mecA gene (carried on the SCCmec mobile genetic element), which encodes PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for methicillin and virtually all other beta-lactams, allowing cell wall synthesis to continue despite drug exposure.

questions.question: A Gram stain performed directly on a clinical specimen (e.g. CSF, sputum, or wound exudate) is valued in the clinical laboratory chiefly because it:
options: Provides definitive species-level identification instantly
Provides rapid, preliminary information on the presence, morphology, and Gram reaction of organisms, guiding immediate empirical therapy while awaiting culture results
Replaces the need for any subsequent culture
Detects viral infections directly
questions.correct_answer: Provides rapid, preliminary information on the presence, morphology, and Gram reaction of organisms, guiding immediate empirical therapy while awaiting culture results
questions.explanation: A direct Gram stain can be performed and reported within minutes, giving clinicians early clues (Gram reaction, cell shape/arrangement, presence of inflammatory cells) that help guide initial empirical antibiotic choice, even though definitive identification and susceptibility require culture.

questions.question: In diagnosing enteric fever (typhoid), blood culture is generally more useful in the first week of illness, while which specimen becomes increasingly useful later in the disease course?
options: Sputum
Stool and urine culture
Cerebrospinal fluid
Sweat
questions.correct_answer: Stool and urine culture
questions.explanation: Salmonella Typhi bacteraemia is typically highest early in typhoid fever, making blood culture most sensitive in week 1; as the disease progresses, the organism is increasingly shed in stool and sometimes urine, so faecal and urine cultures gain diagnostic value in later weeks.

questions.question: The Widal test, historically used in the presumptive serological diagnosis of typhoid fever in resource-limited settings, detects:
options: Antibodies against Salmonella Typhi O and H antigens in the patient's serum
Live Salmonella organisms directly in blood
Antigens of Vibrio cholerae
DNA of Mycobacterium tuberculosis
questions.correct_answer: Antibodies against Salmonella Typhi O and H antigens in the patient's serum
questions.explanation: The Widal test is an agglutination assay measuring the patient's antibody titres against Salmonella Typhi O (somatic) and H (flagellar) antigens; while widely used historically, it has notable limitations in specificity and sensitivity compared with blood culture, the gold standard for typhoid diagnosis.

questions.question: Clostridioides difficile infection, an important cause of healthcare-associated diarrhoea, is typically diagnosed in the clinical laboratory by detecting:
options: Gram stain morphology of stool alone
C. difficile toxins A/B (or the toxin genes/glutamate dehydrogenase antigen) in a diarrhoeal stool specimen from a symptomatic patient, rather than simple culture of the organism
Blood culture only
Sputum culture
questions.correct_answer: C. difficile toxins A/B (or the toxin genes/glutamate dehydrogenase antigen) in a diarrhoeal stool specimen from a symptomatic patient, rather than simple culture of the organism
questions.explanation: Because C. difficile can be carried asymptomatically, diagnosis relies on demonstrating its toxins (or toxin genes, often alongside a GDH antigen screen) in unformed stool from a symptomatic patient, rather than simply culturing the organism, to confirm true toxin-mediated disease.

questions.question: Candida albicans recovered in heavy growth from a catheterised urine specimen in a critically ill patient on broad-spectrum antibiotics most often reflects:
options: A definite, aggressive systemic fungal infection requiring immediate antifungal therapy in every case
Possible catheter-associated colonisation, common in such patients following disruption of normal flora by antibiotics, requiring clinical correlation before treatment decisions
Contamination that should never be reported
Evidence of bacterial urinary tract infection
questions.correct_answer: Possible catheter-associated colonisation, common in such patients following disruption of normal flora by antibiotics, requiring clinical correlation before treatment decisions
questions.explanation: Candiduria in catheterised, antibiotic-treated patients frequently represents colonisation rather than invasive infection, since broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupt competing bacterial flora and catheters provide a surface for yeast growth; clinical correlation (symptoms, risk factors) guides whether treatment is warranted.

questions.question: A 'critical value' or 'panic value' result in the clinical microbiology laboratory, such as a positive blood culture or CSF Gram stain, requires:
options: Routine reporting through standard channels with no urgency
Immediate (often verbal or phone) communication to the requesting clinician, given the potential for rapid patient deterioration if action is delayed
No action until the next working day
Only written documentation, without any direct communication
questions.correct_answer: Immediate (often verbal or phone) communication to the requesting clinician, given the potential for rapid patient deterioration if action is delayed
questions.explanation: Critical/panic values, such as a positive blood culture Gram stain or CSF findings suggestive of meningitis, represent findings that could seriously and rapidly affect patient management; laboratory protocols require these to be communicated to the clinical team immediately, not simply logged for routine reporting.

questions.question: The primary purpose of maintaining a chain of custody and accurate specimen labelling in the clinical microbiology laboratory is to:
options: Satisfy administrative requirements with no real clinical importance
Ensure that results are correctly linked to the right patient, preventing misidentification that could lead to inappropriate treatment of the wrong individual
Slow down laboratory turnaround time deliberately
Avoid the need for quality control testing
questions.correct_answer: Ensure that results are correctly linked to the right patient, preventing misidentification that could lead to inappropriate treatment of the wrong individual
questions.explanation: Accurate specimen labelling and tracking are fundamental to patient safety in clinical microbiology; a mislabelled or misidentified specimen can lead to a result being attributed to the wrong patient, with potentially serious consequences for diagnosis and treatment.

questions.question: Anaerobic blood culture bottles are routinely included alongside aerobic bottles in a standard blood culture set mainly because:
options: Anaerobic organisms are never clinically significant
Certain important bloodstream pathogens (e.g. some Bacteroides, Clostridium species) are obligate or facultative anaerobes that may not grow, or grow poorly, in an aerobic-only bottle
Anaerobic bottles are cheaper and used only for cost reasons
Aerobic bottles cannot detect any bacteria
questions.correct_answer: Certain important bloodstream pathogens (e.g. some Bacteroides, Clostridium species) are obligate or facultative anaerobes that may not grow, or grow poorly, in an aerobic-only bottle
questions.explanation: Some clinically important bloodstream pathogens require anaerobic conditions for optimal or any growth, so paired aerobic and anaerobic blood culture bottles are used to maximise the chance of recovering the full range of possible bacteraemia-causing organisms.

questions.question: Direct antigen detection tests (e.g. rapid group A Streptococcus antigen tests on throat swabs) are valued in clinical microbiology because they:
options: Take several days longer than culture
Provide a rapid result (often within minutes) that can guide immediate treatment decisions, though they are generally less sensitive than culture and a negative result may need confirmation
Are always more accurate than culture for every organism
Require no specimen collection at all
questions.correct_answer: Provide a rapid result (often within minutes) that can guide immediate treatment decisions, though they are generally less sensitive than culture and a negative result may need confirmation
questions.explanation: Rapid antigen tests give near-immediate results useful for point-of-care decision-making, but they typically have lower sensitivity than culture; a negative rapid test in a clinically suspicious case is often followed up with culture for confirmation.

questions.question: Ventilator-associated pneumonia, a healthcare-associated infection in intubated ICU patients, is commonly caused by organisms including:
options: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus aureus, often multidrug-resistant strains typical of the ICU environment
Only Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Exclusively viral pathogens
Helminths
questions.correct_answer: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus aureus, often multidrug-resistant strains typical of the ICU environment
questions.explanation: Ventilator-associated pneumonia is frequently caused by Gram-negative organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Gram-positive Staphylococcus aureus, often with acquired multidrug resistance reflecting the selective pressure of the ICU/hospital environment.

questions.question: In interpreting a wound or skin swab culture result, Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a notable pathogen partly because it can produce a characteristic:
options: Odourless, colourless exudate with no distinguishing features
Blue-green pigment (pyocyanin) and a sweet, grape-like odour, along with resistance to many antibiotics
Chalky white, dry colony with no pigment
Golden-yellow pigment identical to Staphylococcus aureus
questions.correct_answer: Blue-green pigment (pyocyanin) and a sweet, grape-like odour, along with resistance to many antibiotics
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa often produces the blue-green pigment pyocyanin, giving infected wounds a characteristic colour, along with a fruity or grape-like odour from other metabolites, and is notable clinically for intrinsic and acquired resistance to many antimicrobial agents.

questions.question: A common cause of culture-negative but clinically apparent infective endocarditis in resource-limited settings can be fastidious organisms of the HACEK group, which require:
options: No special handling; they grow readily overnight on ordinary media
Prolonged incubation and sometimes enriched media, as they are slow-growing and fastidious, potentially leading to false-negative or delayed standard blood cultures
Only anaerobic conditions and nothing else
Refrigeration of the specimen before plating
questions.correct_answer: Prolonged incubation and sometimes enriched media, as they are slow-growing and fastidious, potentially leading to false-negative or delayed standard blood cultures
questions.explanation: The HACEK group of Gram-negative organisms (associated with endocarditis) are fastidious and slow-growing, sometimes requiring extended incubation (beyond the standard automated blood culture protocol window) and enriched media for reliable recovery, which can otherwise lead to apparently 'culture-negative' endocarditis.

questions.question: Virulence factors that contribute to a microorganism's ability to cause clinical disease include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Adhesins that allow attachment to host tissue
Exotoxins that damage host cells or disrupt normal physiology
Capsules that resist phagocytosis
Complete loss of any ability to grow at human body temperature
questions.correct_answer: Complete loss of any ability to grow at human body temperature
questions.explanation: Adhesins, exotoxins, and antiphagocytic capsules are classic virulence factors that enhance a pathogen's ability to colonise, damage, or evade the host; an organism that cannot grow at body temperature would be unable to establish infection in a human host, so this is not a virulence factor but the opposite.
